propositions.text: This Court granted leave to six sets of parties to start judicial review applications challenging the Governor in Council's approval of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion project.
propositions.quote: On September 4, 2019, this Court granted leave to six sets of parties to start applications for judicial review challenging the Governor in Council’s approval of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion project.

paragraphs.summary: The Court granted leave to six parties to start judicial review applications challenging the Governor in Council's approval of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion project.

propositions.text: The Court's order restricted the applications to three specific questions regarding consultation adequacy, defences or bars, and remedies.
propositions.quote: The Court’s order granting leave restricted the applications to three questions: 1. From August 30, 2018 ... 2. Do any defences or bars to the application apply? 3. If the answers to the questions 1 and 2 are negative, should a remedy be granted and, if so, what remedy and on what terms?

paragraphs.summary: The Court restricted the applications to three questions about consultation adequacy, defences, and remedies.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation filed a notice raising at least seven issues beyond the order's restrictions, totaling more than sixty issues.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation filed a notice of application for judicial review raising these issues. But it raised at least seven others that go beyond the restrictions in the order granting leave ... Tsleil-Waututh Nation raised more than sixty issues—not three.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits Tsleil-Waututh Nation raised over sixty issues, exceeding the three allowed by the Court's order.

propositions.text: The Registry referred the notice to the Court for review under Rule 74, which can remove violating documents and terminate proceedings.
propositions.quote: Because of this, the Registry referred the notice of application to the Court for review under Rule 74. ... As a practical matter, the proceeding is terminated.

paragraphs.summary: The Registry referred the notice to the Court under Rule 74, which can remove violating documents and terminate proceedings.

propositions.text: The Court notified Tsleil-Waututh Nation of the apprehension that its notice violated the leave order and allowed submissions.
propositions.quote: Acting under Rule 74(2) and in accordance with procedural fairness, the Court notified Tsleil-Waututh Nation that the Court apprehended that its notice of application for judicial review went beyond the restrictions in the Order granting leave. The Court gave it and the other parties an opportunity to make submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notified Tsleil-Waututh Nation of the apprehension of violation and allowed submissions.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation violated the leave order seriously and deliberately; an order addressing this violation must be issued.
propositions.quote: Having read and considered the parties’ submissions, the Court concludes that Tsleil-Waututh Nation has violated the Order granting leave. The violation is serious and deliberate. An order must be issued addressing this violation.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Tsleil-Waututh Nation seriously and deliberately violated the leave order and will issue an order.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation submits a panel of judges should decide this matter and that the current judge should not be on the panel.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation submits that a panel of judges should be assigned to decide this matter. Further, it submits that I should not be on that panel.

paragraphs.summary: Tsleil-Waututh Nation argues a panel should decide and the current judge should not sit on it.

propositions.text: The Chief Justice exclusively assigns judges and decides if a single judge or panel hears a matter, except for certain inapplicable restrictions.
propositions.quote: The Chief Justice has the exclusive power to assign judges to matters: Courts Administration Service Act ... Subject to certain restrictions ... none of which apply here, he also has the exclusive power to decide whether a single judge or a panel of judges should hear a matter.

paragraphs.summary: The Chief Justice exclusively assigns judges and decides if a single judge or panel hears a matter, with no applicable restrictions here.

propositions.text: The Chief Justice assigned this judge, who sees no legal reason to recuse, applying Fabrikant test.
propositions.quote: Exercising his powers, the Chief Justice has assigned me to determine this matter. ... I see no legal reason to recuse myself from this matter.

paragraphs.summary: The Chief Justice assigned this judge, who finds no legal reason to recuse under Fabrikant test.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation says the judge is sitting on appeal from own Order, violating subsection 16(4) and natural justice, and is functus officio.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation points out that I was the judge who decided the leave motions ... It says that in this matter, I am now sitting on appeal from my own Order, contrary to subsection 16(4) ... It adds that I am functus officio and cannot revisit the Order.

paragraphs.summary: Tsleil-Waututh Nation alleges the judge is sitting on appeal from own Order, violating law and natural justice, and is functus officio.

propositions.text: The judge is not sitting on appeal or revisiting the Order but deciding if the notice violates the Order's restrictions, taking the Order as valid.
propositions.quote: I am neither sitting on an appeal from my Order nor revisiting it. My task is to decide whether the notice of application for judicial review violates the restrictions in the Order.

paragraphs.summary: The judge clarifies he is not sitting on appeal or revisiting the Order but deciding if the notice violates the Order's restrictions.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation alleges the judge prejudged the Rule 74 review and is biased, relying on prior directions expressing concern about the notice.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation says I have prejudged the outcome of this Rule 74 review. It alleges I am biased. It relies upon directions I issued ...

paragraphs.summary: Tsleil-Waututh Nation alleges the judge prejudged the review and is biased, citing prior directions expressing concern.

propositions.text: The judge denies prejudgment and bias, confirms open-mindedness, and notes ordering a remedy similar to that proposed by Tsleil-Waututh Nation.
propositions.quote: I have not prejudged this review. I am not biased. I confirm that I have been open-minded and persuadable on all issues throughout.

paragraphs.summary: The judge denies prejudgment and bias, confirming open-mindedness and ordering a remedy similar to Tsleil-Waututh Nation's proposal.

propositions.text: Judges must disclose apprehensions about documents to affected parties to allow informed submissions, suspending judgment until submissions are received.
propositions.quote: Judges start by disclosing to affected parties why a document might have to be removed from the court file. ... they suspend their judgment because ... the parties’ submissions may alleviate or eliminate their apprehension.

paragraphs.summary: Judges must disclose apprehensions about documents to parties to allow submissions and suspend judgment until then.

propositions.text: The judge formed an apprehension about the notice's inconsistency with the Order, disclosed it, and sought submissions to enhance fairness and correctness.
propositions.quote: I reviewed the notice ... and formed an apprehension that it was inconsistent with the Order. I disclosed this apprehension ... Far from being evidence of prejudgment or bias, this enhances procedural fairness ...

paragraphs.summary: The judge formed and disclosed apprehension about the notice's inconsistency with the Order to enhance fairness and correctness.

propositions.text: Allegations of bias are serious and require convincing evidence to overcome the presumption of judicial integrity.
propositions.quote: Alleging bias is “a serious step that should not be taken lightly”: R. v. S.(R.D.), ... Only a “serious” and “substantial” demonstration made by “convincing evidence” can reverse the strong presumption that judges will carry out their duties properly and with integrity.

paragraphs.summary: Allegations of bias require serious, substantial, and convincing evidence to overcome judicial integrity presumption.

propositions.text: The bias allegations fall short, should not have been made, and may be abuse of process with consequences considered later.
propositions.quote: Here, the allegations of bias fall way short of the mark and never should have been made ... The consequences ... will be considered at the end of these reasons ...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds bias allegations unfounded, possibly abusive, and will consider consequences later.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation alleges Canada violated the Court's ruling on consultation obligations and must not be allowed to get away with it.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation alleges, among other things, that the Government of Canada has violated the Court’s ruling ... Canada, it suggests, must not be allowed to get away with it.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation's submissions in Rule 74 review ironically defend violating the Court's order restricting issues raised on judicial review.
propositions.quote: Yet in this Rule 74 review, the thrust of Tsleil-Waututh Nation’s submissions is that it is just fine for it to violate the Court’s ruling in Raincoast Conservation that restricted the issues ... The irony is not lost on the Court.

paragraphs.summary: Tsleil-Waututh Nation alleges Canada violated consultation ruling but defends violating the Court's order restricting issues, ironically noted by the Court.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation admits its application raises prohibited issues and wants it viewed as an appeal, though no appeal lies.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation readily admits that its application for judicial review raises issues prohibited by the order granting leave. It wants its application ... to be viewed as an appeal ... even though an appeal does not lie.

propositions.text: Regardless of Tsleil-Waututh Nation's wishes, its application violates the order granting leave.
propositions.quote: Regardless of whatever it wants, the fact remains: its application for judicial review violates the order granting leave.

paragraphs.summary: Tsleil-Waututh Nation admits raising prohibited issues and wants appeal status, but the Court finds the application violates the leave order.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation submits the Court's plenary powers permit hearing an appeal from its own ruling in Raincoast Conservation.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation submits that the plenary or inherent powers of this Court permit it to hear an appeal from this Court’s ruling in Raincoast Conservation.

propositions.text: The Court has plenary powers but they do not extend to creating appeal rights.
propositions.quote: Indeed, this Court has plenary powers: see, e.g., Lee v. Canada ... But they do not extend to the creation of appeal rights.

paragraphs.summary: Tsleil-Waututh Nation argues plenary powers allow appeal from Raincoast ruling, but the Court says plenary powers do not create appeal rights.

propositions.text: Rights to appeal must be authorized by legislation, not inherent or unwritten.
propositions.quote: Rights to appeal are never inherent or unwritten. Instead, impliedly or expressly, they must be authorized by legislation

propositions.text: No implied or express authorization exists for appeal from this Court's order to this Court or from single judge to three-person panel.
propositions.quote: there is no implied or express authorization of any appeal from an order of this Court to this Court, or from a single judge of this Court to a three-person panel of this Court

propositions.text: No such appeal right exists in the Federal Courts Act, Federal Courts Rules, or any other legislation.
propositions.quote: There is no such thing in the Federal Courts Act and the Federal Courts Rules, or in any other legislation for that matter

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no legislative authorization for appeals from single judge to three-person panel in this Court, citing established law that appeal rights must be legislated.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation argues it can appeal the leave order invoking Rule 4 and Society of Composers case.
propositions.quote: In support of its submission that it can appeal the order granting leave, Tsleil-Waututh Nation invokes the gap rule in the Federal Courts Rules (Rule 4), and the case of Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada v. 960122 Ontario Ltd.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits Tsleil-Waututh Nation claims appeal rights based on Rule 4 and Society of Composers case.

propositions.text: Rule 4 allows the Court to provide procedural matters by analogy to Rules or provincial procedural rules when not provided in Rules or Acts.
propositions.quote: Rule 4 allows this Court to provide for a procedural matter not provided for in the Rules or an Act of Parliament by analogy to the Rules or the procedural rules of the province

paragraphs.summary: Rule 4 permits the Court to fill procedural gaps by analogy to Rules or provincial rules.

propositions.text: Court cannot use Rule 4 to create appeal rights out of thin air.
propositions.quote: it is not open to this Court to use Rule 4 to create appeal rights out of thin air

propositions.text: Society of Composers case shows appeal rights can be implicitly authorized by existing legislation, not created anew.
propositions.quote: Society of Composers case... tells us how... an existing legislative provision can implicitly authorize appeal rights

propositions.text: In Society of Composers, appeal rights existed due to Rule 159(1), s. 27 Federal Courts Act, and referee's status as Prothonotary; not created out of thin air.
propositions.quote: Appeal rights were not created out of thin air

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Rule 4 cannot create appeal rights; Society of Composers shows appeal rights must be grounded in existing legislation.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation argues a three-person panel can reverse miscarriage of justice from single judge interlocutory order.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation also submits that a three-person panel of this Court can always reverse a “miscarriage of justice” caused by a single judge’s interlocutory order

propositions.text: This argument fails because appeals require legislative authorization; otherwise any adverse decision could be appealed anytime by claiming miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: This submission is sunk by the principle that appeals are authorised only by legislation... all it has to do is pick up a megaphone and shout “miscarriage of justice”

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues miscarriage of justice allows appeal; court rejects this as appeals require legislative authorization.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation overlooks that single judge orders are orders of the Court under National Energy Board Act.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation overlooks that a single judge making an order under this legislative scheme makes an order of the Court

propositions.text: Once the Court has made an order, it is final except for narrow recourses under Rules 397-399.
propositions.quote: Once the Court... has made an order, the general rule is that it is final. The only exceptions are the narrow recourses for variation, reconsideration or setting aside... under Rules 397-399

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says single judge orders are Court orders; court states such orders are final except for narrow exceptions under Rules 397-399.

propositions.text: This Court never sits in appeal of itself; recourse is to seek leave to appeal to Supreme Court under section 40 Supreme Court Act.
propositions.quote: This Court never sits in appeal of itself. The only recourse... is to seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada under section 40 of the Supreme Court Act

paragraphs.summary: The court states it does not hear appeals of its own orders; parties must seek leave to appeal to Supreme Court.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation cites obiter comment in Abi-Mansour about hearing panels interfering with single judge orders.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation raises the obiter comment in paragraph 4 of Abi-Mansour, above about hearing panels sometimes being able to interfere with the orders of single judges

paragraphs.summary: Respondent cites Abi-Mansour obiter about hearing panels sometimes interfering with single judge orders.

propositions.text: Three-person panel can in rare cases vary interlocutory orders but not by exercising appellate jurisdiction or redressing miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: This Court... in rare circumstances, can make an order that... reverses or varies an interlocutory order... it is not exercising appellate jurisdiction... Nor is it acting... to redress a “miscarriage of justice”

propositions.text: Such variation responds to new circumstances or invitations, e.g., hearing panel interpreting single judge order as permitting action.
propositions.quote: the Court is responding to new circumstances or is accepting an invitation, implied or express, to act

propositions.text: Examples include admitting evidence previously ruled inadmissible or varying procedural rulings at hearing stage.
propositions.quote: Evidence ruled inadmissible by a single judge... may later be admitted... A ruling of a single judge about procedures... can be varied where the hearing panel... considers it appropriate

paragraphs.summary: The court explains panels can vary interlocutory orders in rare cases responding to new circumstances, not by appeal or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: Parliament intended Court to perform a once-and-for-all gatekeeping function on leave motions to ensure only fairly arguable issues proceed.
propositions.quote: Parliament intended this Court to carry out a once-and-for-all “gatekeeping” function when it determines leave motions, to ensure that only fairly arguable issues are litigated

propositions.text: Parliament did not intend all issues raised in leave motion to proceed when only some are fairly arguable.
propositions.quote: Parliament did not intend that all issues raised in a leave motion... should go forward when only three are “fairly arguable”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament intended leave motions to gatekeep so only fairly arguable issues proceed, not all issues.

propositions.text: Parliament can adopt different approaches, e.g., section 58 of Department of Employment and Social Development Act where leave is all-or-nothing.
propositions.quote: Parliament can and sometimes does adopt a different approach... An example... is section 58 of the Department of Employment and Social Development Act... leave is an all-or-nothing proposition

propositions.text: Hillier case illustrates leave is all-or-nothing under that legislative scheme.
propositions.quote: Hillier v. Canada (Attorney General), 2019 FCA 44... leave is an all-or-nothing proposition

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Parliament can require all-or-nothing leave as in Hillier under different legislation.

propositions.text: Courts can screen out issues of insufficient merit in leave process unless legislation says otherwise.
propositions.quote: Unless legislation says otherwise... courts can screen out issues of insufficient merit in the leave-granting process

propositions.text: Cites MacDonald, Wigman, Keegstra, Leroux, Rutherford, Fort MacKay cases supporting screening in leave process.
propositions.quote: MacDonald v. City of Montreal... R. v. Wigman... R. v. Keegstra... Leroux v. TransCanada Pipelines Ltd... Rutherford v. Husky Oil Operations Limited... Fort MacKay First Nation v. Prosper Petroleum Ltd.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites authorities that courts may screen out weak issues in leave motions unless legislation provides otherwise.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation complains Court ignored its arguments in judicial review application, implying negligence.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation complains that the Court has “ignored” the arguments it now advances in its application for judicial review

paragraphs.summary: Respondent complains Court ignored its judicial review arguments, suggesting negligence.

propositions.text: Court has carefully considered many arguments repeatedly with detailed reasons; others found not fairly arguable with reasons.
propositions.quote: many of these arguments have been carefully considered, sometimes repeatedly, accompanied by detailed reasons

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it has carefully considered many arguments with detailed reasons, rejecting some as not fairly arguable.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation’s reassertion of arguments violates leave order and is abuse of process, affecting remedial discretion under Rule 74.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation’s reassertion of these arguments... violates the order granting leave and is an abuse of process

propositions.text: Examples illustrate the nature and significance of this abuse of process.
propositions.quote: Describing a couple of examples of what Tsleil-Waututh Nation is attempting to do sheds light on the nature and significance of this abuse of process

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Tsleil-Waututh Nation’s repeated arguments violate the leave order and constitute abuse of process affecting Rule 74 discretion.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation argues environmental assessment deficiencies require immediate judicial review, not deferred review after Governor in Council decision.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation argues that deficiencies in the environmental assessment process... should be addressed by an immediate judicial review

propositions.text: Court has repeatedly rejected immediate review argument as legislative regime disallows piecemeal judicial reviews; Supreme Court refused leave repeatedly.
propositions.quote: This Court has considered and rejected this argument multiple times... Supreme Court has dismissed leave to appeal from these rulings

propositions.text: Cites Gitxaala Nation, Tsleil-Waututh Nation, Raincoast Conservation cases rejecting automatic invalidation of Governor in Council decision due to NEB process flaws.
propositions.quote: These authorities also clearly and repeatedly reject the proposition... that flaws in the National Energy Board’s environmental assessment process... automatically invalidate the Governor in Council’s decision

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues for immediate review of environmental assessment flaws; court rejects, citing repeated rulings and Supreme Court refusals.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation argues leave order usurps environmental panel role, eviscerates administrative law, permits Governor in Council to ignore law, insulates from judicial scrutiny.
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation advances other arguments against the order granting leave: it “usurp[s] the proper role of the [environmental assessment] panel”, “eviscerate[s]” many “fundamental tenets of administrative law,”...

propositions.text: Appeal from leave order does not lie to this Court; these arguments are not maintainable here but can be raised in Supreme Court leave application.
propositions.quote: An appeal from the order granting leave does not lie to this Court and so these arguments are not maintainable in this Court

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Tsleil-Waututh Nation’s administrative law criticisms cannot be maintained here; appeal lies to Supreme Court only.

propositions.text: Unclear if Tsleil-Waututh Nation seeks variation of leave order; some materials say so but no discussion of Rule 399 or relief sought.
propositions.quote: It is unclear whether Tsleil-Waututh Nation seeks to vary the order granting leave... nowhere does Tsleil-Waututh Nation discuss whether variation can be had in these circumstances under Rule 399

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it unclear if Tsleil-Waututh Nation seeks variation of leave order and notes no discussion of Rule 399 or relief sought.

propositions.text: Nothing raised supports variation of leave order; Rule 399 relief limited to ex parte orders, serious irregularities, new matters, or fraud, none present here.
propositions.quote: nothing Tsleil-Waututh Nation has raised... could possibly support a variation of the order granting leave... None of these circumstances is present here

propositions.text: Variation under Rule 399 is not an appeal: Procter & Gamble Pharmaceuticals v. Canada (Minister of Health).
propositions.quote: Variation under Rule 399 is not an avenue of appeal: Procter & Gamble Pharmaceuticals Canada Inc. v. Canada (Minister of Health)

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no basis for variation of leave order under Rule 399 and notes variation is not an appeal.

propositions.text: Attorney General submits notice of application should be removed under Rule 74; Tsleil-Waututh Nation given one day to file amended notice; respondents two days to comment on compliance.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General of Canada submits that the Court should order the notice of application removed from the court file under Rule 74. He adds that Tsleil-Waututh Nation should be given one day to file an amended notice of application and the respondents two days to make submissions on whether the amended application complies with the Order granting leave

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits notice of application should be removed under Rule 74 with time for amended filing and submissions on compliance.

propositions.text: Trans Mountain respondents submit notice of application should be removed under Rule 74
propositions.quote: The Trans Mountain respondents similarly submit that the notice of application for judicial review should be removed from the court file under Rule 74.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation should not be allowed to refile application
propositions.quote: They suggest this is a proper response to a severe abuse of process and deliberate violation of a court order.

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue for removal of notice under Rule 74 and oppose refiling due to abuse of process and court order violation.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation asks to amend notice under Rule 75 but has not moved or submitted amendments
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation asks that the Court permit it to amend its notice of application for judicial review under Rule 75. But it has not moved for that relief. Nor has it submitted its proposed amendments for the Court’s consideration.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation's inaction is mystifying given expedited nature of challenges
propositions.quote: Given the “highly expedited” manner in which the challenges to the Governor in Council’s approval of the pipeline project are to proceed (see Raincoast Conservation at para. 76), its inaction is mystifying.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks amendment but has not moved or submitted amendments; court finds inaction mystifying given expedited process.

propositions.text: Three considerations affect the Court’s remedial discretion
propositions.quote: Three considerations affect the Court’s remedial discretion.

paragraphs.summary: Court states three considerations affect its remedial discretion.

propositions.text: Removal under Rule 74 is not a ruling on merits and no res judicata arises
propositions.quote: First, the removal of the notice of application for judicial review under Rule 74 would not be a ruling on the merits of the judicial review. In legal parlance, there would be no res judicata.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation could file a corrected application if it acts quickly
propositions.quote: Provided that Tsleil-Waututh Nation acted quickly, it could file another, corrected, application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds removal under Rule 74 is not on merits and Tsleil-Waututh could refile if acting quickly.

propositions.text: Deliberate violation of court order is serious and can be contempt of court
propositions.quote: Second, violation of a court order, particularly the sort of deliberate, defiant violation we have here, is most serious. It is an attack on the rule of law. In some circumstances it can constitute contempt of court and be punishable by some of the toughest sanctions known to our law.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh’s relitigation and attack on court impartiality are further abuses of process
propositions.quote: The seriousness is compounded by Tsleil-Waututh’s penchant for relitigation and its unmeritorious attack on the impartiality of the Court, two further abuses of process.

propositions.text: Remedies for abuse of process aim to redress abuse, not punish transgressor
propositions.quote: But remedies for abuse of process should be aimed at redressing the abuse, not punishing the transgressor, no matter how substandard its conduct may be: see, e.g., R. v. Carosella, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 80, 142 D.L.R. (4th) 595.

propositions.text: Court agrees conduct is worthy of denunciation but preventing challenge is excessive now
propositions.quote: The Court agrees with the Trans Mountain respondents that Tsleil-Waututh Nation’s conduct is worthy of denunciation. But preventing it from challenging the Governor in Council’s decision seems, at this time, excessive.

propositions.text: Assessment could change depending on future events
propositions.quote: Depending on what happens later, this assessment could change.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds deliberate violation serious and abusive but remedy should redress not punish; preventing challenge now is excessive but may change.

propositions.text: Rule 74 only allows removal of document from court file
propositions.quote: Third, this is a Rule 74 review. In terms of remedy, Rule 74 is limited: it provides only for the removal of a document from the court file.

propositions.text: Court may vary a rule under Rule 55 in special circumstances
propositions.quote: But under Rule 55, the Court may vary a rule in “special circumstances”. Through this mechanism, other remedies may be available in a Rule 74 review.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Rule 74 limits remedy to removal but Rule 55 allows variation in special circumstances.

propositions.text: Five other judicial review applications of Governor in Council’s decision are before Court
propositions.quote: Five other applications for judicial review of the Governor in Council’s decision are before the Court.

propositions.text: Court made procedural and scheduling order on September 20, 2019 to expedite and consolidate applications
propositions.quote: On September 20, 2019, this Court made a procedural and scheduling order governing them. That order expedites and consolidates the applications and sets short timelines for the pre-hearing procedures, all to further the public interest in having the matter determined quickly.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes five other applications and a procedural order to expedite and consolidate them for public interest.

propositions.text: Public interest in expedited resolution is paramount
propositions.quote: In these circumstances, the public interest is paramount.

propositions.text: Many parties and much of Canada await Court’s verdict urgently
propositions.quote: One way or the other, the parties in the consolidated proceedings—to say nothing of a good chunk of the population of Canada—await this Court’s ultimate verdict. A verdict is urgently needed.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds public interest in expedited verdict is paramount and many await it urgently.

propositions.text: Removing Tsleil-Waututh’s notice would cause complicated delays and frustrate public interest
propositions.quote: Removing Tsleil-Waututh Nation’s notice of application from the court file and closing the court file would set in motion a complicated, potentially time-consuming chain of events that could undercut the objectives of the procedural and scheduling order, causing delay and frustrating the public interest.

propositions.text: Procedural order would need amendment to remove Tsleil-Waututh Nation
propositions.quote: First, the procedural and scheduling order would have to be amended to remove Tsleil-Waututh Nation from the consolidated proceedings.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation could start a new application for judicial review
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation would then be able to start a new application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Court would scrutinize new notice for compliance with September 4, 2019 Order
propositions.quote: The Court would then have to scrutinize the new notice of application to ensure it complies with the September 4, 2019 Order.

propositions.text: Submissions may be invited and considered on compliance
propositions.quote: It may be necessary to invite and consider submissions on that point.

propositions.text: If compliant, Tsleil-Waututh must move to consolidate new application with consolidated proceedings
propositions.quote: If the new application is compliant, Tsleil-Waututh Nation would have to bring a motion to consolidate its application for judicial review with the consolidated proceedings.

propositions.text: Additional time and submissions may be required, causing delays
propositions.quote: Additional time may be required to receive submissions on that. Delays in the filing of evidence in the consolidated proceedings may result, ultimately pushing back the hearing of this matter, currently scheduled for the week of December 16, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds removing notice would cause delays, amendments, scrutiny, motions, submissions, and push back hearing, frustrating public interest.

propositions.text: Special circumstances warrant varying Rule 74 to allow filing amended notice complying with leave order
propositions.quote: These special circumstances warrant varying Rule 74 to allow for a different remedy: Tsleil-Waututh Nation should be given an opportunity to file an amended notice of application for judicial review that complies with the restrictions in the order granting leave.

propositions.text: Allowing amendment reduces need for multiple submissions and allows participation if compliant
propositions.quote: This will reduce the need for other parties to file multiple sets of submissions and, as long as the amended notice of application is compliant, will allow Tsleil-Waututh Nation to participate in the consolidated proceedings.

propositions.text: Court will impose tight timelines on amendment process as suggested by Attorney General
propositions.quote: The Court will impose tight timelines on this process, along the lines suggested by the Attorney General of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Court varies Rule 74 to allow amendment with tight timelines to reduce submissions and allow participation if compliant.

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh Nation must appeal orders properly or use Rules 397-399; defiance and relitigation not allowed
propositions.quote: In the future, if Tsleil-Waututh Nation is dissatisfied with an order, it must appeal it by following proper, legislative avenues or make use of the narrow recourses in Rules 397-399. Defiance is not an option. Nor is relitigation.

paragraphs.summary: Court orders Tsleil-Waututh to appeal properly or use rules; defiance and relitigation prohibited.

propositions.text: Squamish Nation adopts Tsleil-Waututh Nation’s submissions
propositions.quote: Late in this process, Squamish Nation filed submissions adopting those of Tsleil-Waututh Nation.

propositions.text: Squamish Nation concedes its notice also raises restricted issues
propositions.quote: It concedes that its notice of application for judicial review also raises issues restricted by the order granting leave.

propositions.text: Squamish’s notice is less non-compliant but must be brought into compliance
propositions.quote: Its notice of application is not as badly out of compliance as that of Tsleil-Waututh Nation. Nevertheless, its notice must also be brought into compliance.

propositions.text: Public interest requires Squamish to comply on same timelines as Tsleil-Waututh
propositions.quote: The public interest in expedition requires that it do so on the same timelines as Tsleil-Waututh Nation.

paragraphs.summary: Squamish adopts Tsleil-Waututh’s submissions, concedes restricted issues, must comply on same timelines for public interest.

propositions.text: Order: Tsleil-Waututh and Squamish to file amended notices by Sept 26, 2019 4pm PDT
propositions.quote: Within one day (by 4 pm PDT on Thursday, September 26, 2019) Tsleil-Waututh Nation and Squamish Nation shall each file an amended notice of application for judicial review that complies with the restrictions in the order granting leave;

propositions.text: Other parties may file representations by Sept 30, 2019 10am PDT on compliance
propositions.quote: All other parties may file representations by 10 am PDT on Monday, September 30, 2019 on whether the amended notices of application comply with the restrictions in the order granting leave;

propositions.text: Tsleil-Waututh and Squamish may file replies by Oct 1, 2019 noon PDT
propositions.quote: Tsleil-Waututh Nation and Squamish Nation may each file a reply by noon PDT on Tuesday, October 1, 2019;

propositions.text: Service and filing per procedural and scheduling order of Sept 20, 2019
propositions.quote: Service shall be performed in accordance with the procedural and scheduling order dated September 20, 2019 and filing shall be made by delivering to the email address in that order;

propositions.text: Court remains seized to deal with amended notices and make further orders if needed
propositions.quote: The Court remains seized with this matter to deal with the amended notices of application for judicial review and to make any further order necessary in the circumstances, especially if the amended notices of application for judicial review do not comply with the restrictions in the order granting leave;

propositions.text: Timelines in procedural and scheduling order of Sept 20, 2019 remain in effect
propositions.quote: The timelines set out in the Court’s procedural and scheduling order of September 20, 2019 remain in effect.

paragraphs.summary: Court orders amended notices by Sept 26, representations by Sept 30, replies by Oct 1, service per order, remains seized, timelines remain.

propositions.text: Attorney General requests costs payable forthwith due to Tsleil-Waututh’s submissions
propositions.quote: The Attorney General of Canada requests its costs of this Rule 74 review payable forthwith in any event of the cause. Its costs are attributable to the submissions of Tsleil-Waututh Nation, not the brief, late submissions of Squamish Nation.

propositions.text: Costs of $2,000 payable by Tsleil-Waututh to Attorney General ordered
propositions.quote: Thus, I will order costs to the Attorney General in the fixed amount of $2,000, all-inclusive, payable by Tsleil-Waututh Nation forthwith in any event of the cause.

propositions.text: Trans Mountain respondents did not request costs
propositions.quote: The Trans Mountain respondents did not request costs.

paragraphs.summary: Attorney General requests costs due to Tsleil-Waututh; court orders $2,000 costs payable by Tsleil-Waututh; Trans Mountain did not request costs.
